title: Egogram

source.quote: The idea is to draw a vertical bar above each ego-state label. The height of the bar shows how much of the time you use that functional part.

setting: Saturday morning. A group chat is planning a long-weekend trip. Zara, the self-appointed organizer, has just sent a wall of text.
playAs: Leo, Zara's oldest friend in the group

L1.line: We're doing the beach house, not the city. Obviously. Someone has to decide, since no one else ever will. Don't argue, I've already booked it. You'll thank me later.
cues: already booked it before asking anyone
no room left for anyone else's input
L1.question: Across this whole message, which functional ego state is dominant in Zara - and is it the positive or negative side?

options.feedback: Positive CP directs toward someone else's good and leaves room to object; here Zara's already booked it and shut down argument before it started - that's not protection, that's control for its own sake.
Right. "Don't argue", booking it without asking, and the flat finality are negative Controlling Parent - directing others while discounting their say in it.
Free Child would be spontaneous and uncensored, but not aimed at controlling someone else's choices - Zara isn't playing, she's issuing a verdict.
There's no here-and-now weighing of options or information exchange here - just a decision already made and defended against argument. That's Parent content, not Adult process.

L1.lesson: An egogram isn't read off a single line - it's which functional part keeps showing up. Four sentences of "obviously", pre-booking, and "don't argue" is a consistent Controlling Parent pattern, and the total absence of any bid for others' input marks it negative rather than positive.

L2.intro: The group chat goes quiet after Zara's message. What do you say?

beats.line: So - beach house. Everyone's fine with that, right?
cues: tone expects agreement, not an answer

options.text: Sounds great, Zara, you always sort us out!
options.outcome: Zara relaxes - and books the next three trips the exact same way, unasked, as usual.
options.lesson: Praising the takeover from Adapted Child invites more of the same negative Controlling Parent pattern - it feels easier in the moment but reinforces the imbalance.

options.text: Beach house works for me, but can we check with Priti and Dev before it's final?
options.outcome: A pause, then: "Oh - sure, I'll ask them." The decision stands, but the process opens up.
options.lesson: Naming the missing step - did anyone else actually get asked - from Adult doesn't attack Zara's choice, it corrects the process. That's exactly the kind of challenge that can shift someone's egogram over time.

options.text: You can't just decide everything for everyone, Zara.
options.outcome: Zara goes quiet, then: "Fine. Forget it, you guys plan it then." Control for control - now someone else has to do the work she was doing.
options.lesson: Matching Controlling Parent with Controlling Parent crosses the transaction, but it's judgment for judgment rather than a request - it can get someone to back off, at a cost.

options.text: Whatever, it's not worth the fight.
options.outcome: The trip gets booked Zara's way, again. Quiet surface, same pattern underneath.
options.lesson: Negative Adapted Child compliance keeps the peace short-term but does nothing to change the recurring pattern - the egogram stays exactly where it was.

fields.label: Draw the vector for Zara's message, and for Leo's best response.
In under 60 words, describe your own egogram today: which functional part gets the tallest bar, and is it serving you right now?

echo.setting: 24 hours later: Leo catches himself mid-sentence, telling his own partner where they're eating tonight without asking.
echo.line: We're going to the new ramen place. Obviously. I already booked it.
echo.shape: same egogram-reading shape as L1, turned on the player's own pattern
